# Organizations, SCPs, Control Tower and RAM: say it

<!-- speak:start id=organizations-s01 -->
### Prompt 1

**A customer asks.** How do I make sure that even a production administrator cannot turn off the audit log?

<details>
<summary>Answer</summary>

**In 10 seconds.** Use an organization trail from the management account. Member accounts, their administrators included, can see the trail but can't change or delete it.

**In 60 seconds.**

The short answer is: make the audit log an organization trail in the management account.

It works like this. One organization trail logs every account.

Member accounts can see that trail, but they can't change it or delete it.

That includes the production administrator, because production is a member account.

Keep the log files in a separate log archive account, protected from changes.

For other rules, add a service control policy that denies the action.

Even an administrator with full access can't use an action that the SCP blocks.

The thing to watch is the management account itself.

SCPs don't limit the users or roles in that account.

Keep workloads out of it, and give very few people access.

In your case, production stays a member account, so its administrators can't change the trail.

Who can sign in to the management account today?

**Skeleton.** organization trail from management account / members see it, can't change / SCP deny beats AdministratorAccess / management account outside SCPs

**Must say.**

- An organization trail logs events for all accounts, and member accounts can see it but cannot modify or delete it.
- You create an organization trail from the management account or a delegated administrator account.
- If an SCP above the account blocks a permission, users and roles in that account cannot use it, even with AdministratorAccess.
- SCPs do not restrict users or roles in the management account, so AWS recommends keeping resources out of it.

**Do not say.**

- "an SCP on the root also stops the management account from changing the trail". Say: SCPs affect only member accounts. They do not restrict users or roles in the management account.
- "the production account can't even see the organization trail". Say: Member accounts can see the organization trail, but they cannot modify or delete it.
- "an administrator with AdministratorAccess in production can turn the SCP off for that account". Say: If an SCP above the account blocks a permission, users and roles in that account cannot use it, even with AdministratorAccess.

**Follow-up questions.**

- What if someone deletes the log bucket instead of the trail? In a Control Tower landing zone, mandatory controls on the Security OU prevent deletion of the S3 buckets that Control Tower creates in the log archive account. From Landing Zone version 4.0, check that they are applied: they are no longer applied by default.
- Can the people in the management account change the trail? SCPs do not restrict them, and Control Tower preventive controls are not applied to the management account. Their actions are still logged, so keep very few people there.

</details>
<!-- speak:end -->

<!-- speak:start id=organizations-s02 -->
### Prompt 2

**A customer asks.** Do we need AWS Control Tower, or is AWS Organizations enough?

<details>
<summary>Answer</summary>

**In 10 seconds.** Both manage many accounts. Organizations is the framework. Control Tower builds and governs the accounts on top of it, with ready-made controls.

**In 60 seconds.**

Both help you run many AWS accounts from one place.

The difference is that Control Tower builds and governs the accounts for you.

It works like this. Organizations is the framework: accounts, organizational units, policies and one bill.

Control Tower is the automation and governance layer on top of it.

It builds a landing zone, a well-architected environment of many accounts.

Account Factory creates each new account from a template, with controls applied.

The thing to watch is cost. Control Tower has no charge of its own.

But you pay for the services it turns on, like AWS Config.

Short-lived resources, like Spot workers, can raise the AWS Config bill.

In your case, size decides. AWS suggests Control Tower for more than a handful of accounts.

How many accounts will you have next year, and who will create them?

**Skeleton.** both run many accounts / Organizations framework, Control Tower layer / landing zone, Account Factory, controls / no charge, but AWS Config

**Must say.**

- AWS describes Organizations as the framework and Control Tower as the automation and governance layer on top of it.
- Control Tower extends the capabilities of AWS Organizations and applies controls to keep accounts from drifting away from best practices.
- Account Factory is a configurable account template that automates applying controls and policies to new accounts.
- Control Tower has no additional charge, but you pay for the services it enables, such as AWS Config and CloudTrail.
- AWS says that with more than a handful of accounts, an orchestration layer such as Control Tower helps with account deployment and governance.

**Do not say.**

- "Control Tower replaces Organizations, so you pick one of the two". Say: Control Tower extends the capabilities of AWS Organizations. It works on top of Organizations, not instead of it.
- "Control Tower costs nothing to run". Say: Control Tower has no additional charge, but you pay for the services it enables, such as AWS Config and CloudTrail.

**Follow-up questions.**

- Can we add Control Tower later, to the organization we already have? Yes. You register the existing OUs and enroll the existing accounts. Until you do, accounts and OUs created outside Control Tower are not bound by its controls.
- Do the Control Tower controls stop a bad action, or only report it? It depends on the type. Preventive controls prevent actions from occurring. Detective controls detect events when they occur and alert through the dashboard. Proactive controls check resources before they are provisioned.

</details>
<!-- speak:end -->
